scenes.heading: Resilience in Distributed Systems
scenes.narration: Let's talk about resilience: the discipline of containing failure so one sick dependency doesn't take down your whole service.

scenes.heading: Every network call will fail
items: The only questions are how often, and whether it spreads
No single trick — a few composable patterns do it
Goal: keep a partial outage partial
scenes.narration: In a distributed system every network call will fail; the only questions are how often, and whether that failure spreads. Resilience is the discipline of containing failure so one sick dependency doesn't cascade into a total outage. No single trick does it. Instead a small set of composable patterns, layered together, keeps a partial outage partial.

scenes.heading: The patterns compose into one story
steps: Retries with backoff + jitter recover transient blips
A circuit breaker stops hammering a dead dependency
Load shedding + backpressure protect you under overload
scenes.narration: The patterns compose into one story. Timeouts bound every wait, so a hang can't leak resources. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter recover from transient blips without amplifying them into a retry storm. A circuit breaker stops hammering a dependency that's clearly down, turning slow timeouts into instant failures. Bulkheads cap the resources any one dependency can consume. And load shedding with backpressure protects you when overload arrives.

scenes.heading: The circuit breaker in Go
scenes.narration: Here's a minimal circuit breaker. It has three states. While open, it fails fast and doesn't even attempt the call. Otherwise it tries, and on each failure it increments a counter; once that counter crosses a threshold, it trips open for a cooldown. After the cooldown it goes half-open to probe with a trial request, and a success resets the counter and closes the circuit. This is what converts a slow, timing-out dependency into an instant, cheap failure.

scenes.text: Retries without backoff, jitter, and idempotency checks amplify outages and can corrupt data.
scenes.narration: A crucial warning: retries do not always make a system more reliable. Without backoff and jitter, a thousand clients retry in lockstep and turn a blip into a self-inflicted denial of service. And without idempotency and error classification, you might retry a non-idempotent write and double-charge a customer, or keep retrying a deterministic 400 that will never succeed. Retries need guardrails.

scenes.text: Layer timeout, retry, breaker, bulkhead, and shedding — negligible cost, dramatically better tail latency.
scenes.narration: Layered together, timeout, then retry, then breaker, behind a bulkhead, in front of load shedding, these patterns add negligible per-call overhead but massively improve tail latency and stability under stress. They factor cleanly into reusable wrappers like a resilient HTTP client, keeping business logic clean while making failure behavior explicit, testable, and tunable per dependency.
